briefing.text: The hypothesis is about pathway ACTIVATION, not just mutation presence. Finding ARAF N217I/G322S in the mutation table only shows the variants exist; activation needs a readout such as expression or pathway scores, phospho-ERK/MEK, or a functional assay. Before choosing a label, list every file and column and record whether any variable measures pathway activity. Decide whether the claim can be tested from what is actually there.
briefing.reason: This is the main framing risk. A team could read 'variant present' as support, or 'no association' as contradiction, without checking that the data measure the outcome the hypothesis is about.

briefing.text: The cohort is very small (about a dozen iCCA samples) and probably has only one or two ARAF carriers. A non-significant test at this size cannot show that ARAF mutations fail to activate the pathway, because absence of evidence is not evidence against. Count the samples and carriers first, and only treat a direct contradicting measurement as evidence against the claim.
briefing.reason: This stops the team from reading an underpowered null result as contradiction.

briefing.text: Known activating ARAF mutations cluster at the CR2 S214 hotspot (S214C/P) and in beta3-alphaC in-frame deletions. In deep mutational scans most other ARAF missense variants lower MAPK activity, so variants such as N217I or G322S are of unknown significance by default. Check the Hotspot and annotation columns for the ARAF rows, and do not treat a missense call as activating unless something in the data says so.
briefing.reason: This is domain knowledge the team cannot get from the data, and it changes how much weight a bare ARAF missense call can carry.

briefing.text: Protein positions depend on the transcript, so N217I or G322S may be missing, listed at a different residue, or listed under another gene. Filter data_mutations.txt for Hugo_Symbol == ARAF and inspect HGVSp_Short, Protein_position, Transcript_ID, HGVSc and Tumor_Sample_Barcode. Report exactly which variants exist and in which samples, and do not treat a different residue as the variant named in the hypothesis.
briefing.reason: This makes sure the team checks that the specific variants are actually present before reasoning about them.

briefing.text: ARAF-mutant samples may also carry other MAPK drivers (FGFR2 fusions, KRAS/BRAF/NRAS mutations), and any pathway state in those samples could not be credited to ARAF. Cross-tabulate ARAF carriers against these alterations and against TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS. Check DNA_support in data_sv.txt, since RNA-only fusions can be read-through artefacts. With n around 12 and possible high-TMB samples, mutual-exclusivity patterns are descriptive only. They are not evidence for or against shared pathway activation.
briefing.reason: This stops the team from using co-occurrence or exclusivity patterns as stand-ins for activation.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed 'the pathway' means the RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK (MAPK) pathway and limited their co-alteration scan to a hand-picked MAPK gene list; the hypothesis does not name the pathway, and neither team tested whether the conclusion depends on that gene list.

Both teams assumed that the only thing that could count as evidence about 'activation' is a direct activity readout (expression, phospho-protein). Neither team spelled out whether Hotspot=0 or other annotation content could count as evidence *against* activation (which would point to False), as opposed to simply having no readout (Not verifiable).

Both teams treated every row in data_mutations.txt as a confirmed somatic tumour mutation. But Mutation_Status, Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode and all read-count columns are empty, and 66/218 rows carry a dbSNP ID, so somatic status and clonality of the two ARAF calls were never checked.
unused_evidence: The t_ref_count/t_alt_count/n_ref_count/n_alt_count columns are fully empty, and so are Mutation_Status and Matched_Norm_Sample_Barcode. This means variant allele fraction and somatic status cannot be assessed for the ARAF calls. Neither team reported this, though it affects whether 'presence' is even established.
Annotation_Status/Hotspot: 6 rows have FAILED annotation (Hotspot=FAILED). Team B did not report whether its MAPK scan covered those rows, and Team A checked Hotspot only for the ARAF rows.

The SV table has RIN1 (a RAS effector) fusions in three samples, including ICC12 (RIN1-IGLL5), which is an ARAF G322S carrier. Both teams reported 'no other MAPK alterations in carriers' without saying whether RAS-effector or other pathway genes outside their list were considered. All SVs are RNA-only.
Chromosome X location of ARAF together with the absence of a sex variable in data_clinical_patient.txt: zygosity/hemizygosity of the variants cannot be judged. Neither team noted this.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A's weakest point (activation may have been shown by functional experiments outside these data) was only reported, not resolved. The team gave no reason why the absence of a readout means 'Not verifiable' rather than 'cannot support, therefore False'.
Team B's weakest point (whether presence alone should count as support) was only reported. Team B listed no pitfalls_checked at all, and its MAPK gene list is not recorded.

Neither team resolved the library's note that most ARAF missense variants outside the S214 hotspot reduce MAPK activity. Whether non-hotspot status in the data counts as contradicting evidence or as no evidence was left implicit.
second_readings: 'Activation of the pathway' could mean any signalling pathway ARAF belongs to, not only MAPK. The scope of the co-alteration scan depends on this reading.

The hypothesis could be read as two parts: (a) ARAF N217I and G322S occur in iCCA, which the data can test, and (b) they activate the pathway, which needs a functional readout. One label must cover a claim that is half testable, so it matters whether 'partially testable' maps to Not verifiable or to a verdict on the testable part.

'ARAF mutations' could refer to the two named variants only or to all ARAF mutations in the cohort. The teams found exactly the two named ones, but neither stated whether any other ARAF rows exist (for example in FAILED-annotation rows).
challenge.verdict: I moderately trust the agreed 'Not verifiable'. I checked the files: there is no expression, phospho or functional variable, and both named variants appear only as unvalidated, non-hotspot WXS calls. The main risk is not a missed readout but the label boundary: whether non-hotspot status or the half-testable claim should push the label to False or True, and neither team argued that explicitly.

questions.question: In the cBioPortal mutation data format, which fields indicate somatic versus germline status and allele fraction? What does it mean when Mutation_Status and the tumour/normal read-count fields are all blank?
questions.why: This determines whether the presence of the variants as somatic events is established at all, and neither team addressed it.

questions.question: For a hypothesis that combines a testable presence claim with an untestable functional-effect claim, how do common evaluation conventions for data-driven hypothesis verification assign a support / contradict / not-verifiable label?

findings.question: In the cBioPortal mutation data format, which fields indicate somatic versus germline status and allele fraction? What does it mean when Mutation_Status and the tumour/normal read-count fields are all blank?
findings.answer: Mutation_Status is the per-row somatic/germline field. It is optional: cBioPortal shows 'Somatic' or 'Germline' in the Mutations tab, does not load rows marked None, LOH or Wildtype, and shows any other value as plain text. Allele fraction comes from t_ref_count and t_alt_count, the reads supporting the reference and variant allele in the tumour (VAF = t_alt/(t_ref+t_alt)). n_ref_count and n_alt_count give the same counts for the matched normal; cBioPortal stores these four as tumor/normal_ref/alt_count. All of these columns are optional. When they are blank, the file just does not record somatic status or read support. The row is still a loaded mutation call, and cBioPortal mutation profiles are conventionally somatic calls, so blanks do not mean the variant is germline or absent. But somatic origin, VAF/clonality and whether normal reads show the variant cannot be checked from the data. The presence of the variants is therefore established only as the study's reported calls, not as independently confirmed somatic events. This conclusion is my inference from the column definitions; no page states it outright.
findings.confidence: high for the field definitions; medium for what blanks mean

findings.question: For a hypothesis that combines a testable presence claim with an untestable functional-effect claim, how do common evaluation conventions for data-driven hypothesis verification assign a support / contradict / not-verifiable label?
findings.answer: In FEVER-style verification, SUPPORTED and REFUTED both need evidence for the claim; anything else is NOT ENOUGH INFO. Under the closed-world rule, a claim is accepted only if every asserted part is supported. For a compound claim: (a) if any testable part is contradicted, e.g. the named variants are absent, the label is Refuted/False. (b) If the presence part is supported but no variable in the data bears on the functional or activation part, the claim is not Supported. It is not Refuted either, so the label is NOT ENOUGH INFO, which maps to 'Not verifiable'. One paper (arXiv 2604.10990) calls accepting a claim because its most visible part checks out 'salient-constraint checking' and treats it as a shortcut, not proper verification. HoVer notes that Refuted vs NotEnoughInfo is often ambiguous for multi-part claims and merges them into Not-Supported. No source I read was specific to cancer-genomics hypothesis labelling, so mapping these conventions onto this task's labels is an analogy.
